newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania says on right track to stem corruption.
newsitem.headline: Romania says on right track to stem corruption.

text.p: Romania's president said on Thursday that his new centrist administration had turned the corner in its fight against corruption, which had caused huge losses to the economy and threatened to throw the Balkan country into chaos last year.

"We have avoided a very serious threat, which faces several countries around us, that the state should be replaced and led by Mafia-like structures," Emil Constantinescu told a news conference marking 200 days since he took office.
Constantinescu said the fight against organised crime, fraud and corruption, which spread like wildfire in the Balkan country after the 1989 overthrow of communism, had been successful.
"If things had continued the way they did last year, Romania would have been destroyed through the failure of its economic system, which was on the verge of collapse," he said.
Romania's new centrist authorities, elected last November, inherited from the former leftists a system marred by fraud and corruption which touched almost every corner of daily life.
"We've stopped the terrible haemorrhage produced through the banking system...a corrupt and non-functional system in customs and taxation," Constantinescu said.

He said tax evasion amounted to some 1.57 trillion lei ($927 million) in the first half of 1997. Of this, 572 billion $336.6 million) had been returned to the state budget with help from the financial police.
The funds secured so far from the anti-corrption drive amounted to what Constantinescu said was half the state budget for culture, education, youth and sports.

The fight against crime and graft had been one of the main pillars of Constantinescu's 200-day Contract with Romania -- the legislative basis to build a new type of state and society -- presented during his 1996 electoral campaign.

"We will take no account of social position, wealth, political orientation or connections. We will observe only the law," Constantinescu said last year. And he showed he meant businesss after being sworn in office six months ago.

The national police has sacked a quarter of its county chiefs since. Prosecutors have probed cases of corruption involving leading businessmen and politicians and the financial police have recouped tens of million of dollars in unpaid taxes.
"There were terrible losses," Constantinescu told the news conference, adding that he had been shocked at the size and extent of the shady deals revealed by police investigations.
Romania's black market economy was estimated to rob the country's budget of 30 percent of its GDP in 1996, data showed.
Putting corrupt bankers and politicians into jail or out of office had a good effect on public opinion and had helped authorities restore their credibility, Constantinescu said.
"It is a long and difficult process. All the steps have been taken in keeping with the constitution and laws," he said.
